claim: Fission yeast condensin accumulates at telomere repeats through the balancing acts of Taz1 and Mit1.
source: Here, we show that fission yeast condensin accumulates at telomere repeats through the balancing acts of Taz1, a core component of the shelterin complex that ensures telomeric functions, and Mit1, a nucleosome remodeler associated with shelterin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR experiments showing condensin localization at telomeres and its dependence on Taz1 and Mit1.

claim: Condensin takes part in sister-telomere separation in anaphase.
source: We further show that condensin takes part in sister-telomere separation in anaphase, and that this event can be uncoupled from the prior separation of chromosome arms, implying a telomere-specific separation mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing telomere separation defects in condensin mutants and by experiments demonstrating that telomere separation can occur independently of chromosome arm separation.

claim: Sister-telomere separation can be uncoupled from the prior separation of chromosome arms.
source: We further show that condensin takes part in sister-telomere separation in anaphase, and that this event can be uncoupled from the prior separation of chromosome arms, implying a telomere-specific separation mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with top2-250 mutant cells showing that telomeres can separate even when chromosome arms remain entangled.

claim: Increasing or decreasing condensin occupancy specifically at telomeres modifies accordingly the efficiency of their separation in anaphase.
source: Consistent with a cis-acting process, increasing or decreasing condensin occupancy specifically at telomeres modifies accordingly the efficiency of their separation in anaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that taz1Δ (which decreases condensin at telomeres) worsens telomere separation defects in cut3-477 mutants, while mit1Δ (which increases condensin at telomeres) rescues these defects.

claim: Condensin promotes sister-telomere separation by counteracting cohesin.
source: Genetic evidence suggests that condensin promotes sister-telomere separation by counteracting cohesin.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that the rad21-K1 cohesin mutant accelerates telomere separation and rescues telomere separation defects in condensin mutants, and by ChIP data showing increased cohesin at telomeres in condensin mutants.

claim: Condensin is a ring-shaped ATPase complex that belongs to the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) family of genome organizers.
source: Condensin is a ring-shaped ATPase complex that belongs to the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) family of genome organizers, which also includes the cohesin complex involved in chromatin folding during interphase and in sister-chromatid cohesion (Hirano, 2016; Davidson and Peters, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on condensin structure and function.

claim: Condensin is composed of a core ATPase heterodimer made of the SMC2 and SMC4 proteins, associated with a kleisin and two HEAT-repeat subunits.
source: Condensin is composed of a core ATPase heterodimer, made of the SMC2 and SMC4 proteins, associated with a kleisin and two HEAT-repeat subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about condensin complex composition.

claim: Most multicellular eukaryotes possess two condensin variants, named condensin I and II, made of a same SMC2/4 core but associated with distinct sets of non-SMC subunits.
source: Most multicellular eukaryotes possess two condensin variants, named condensin I and II, made of a same SMC2/4 core but associated with distinct sets of non-SMC subunits (Ono et al., 2003; Hirano, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing condensin variants.

claim: Budding and fission yeasts possess a single condensin complex, similar to condensin I.
source: Budding and fission yeasts, in contrast, possess a single condensin complex, similar to condensin I.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about condensin complexes in yeast species.

claim: Condensin shapes mitotic chromosomes by massively binding to DNA upon mitotic entry and by folding chromatin into arrays of loops.
source: There is robust evidence that condensin shapes mitotic chromosomes by massively binding to DNA upon mitotic entry and by folding chromatin into arrays of loops (Gibcus et al., 2018; Kakui et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating condensin's role in chromosome folding.

claim: Condensin reduces the length of chromosomes, confers to chromosome arms the stiffness to withstand the spindle traction forces, and promotes the removal of catenations between chromosomes and sister-chromatids.
source: Thereby, condensin conceivably reduces the length of chromosomes, confers to chromosome arms the stiffness to withstand the spindle traction forces (Sun et al., 2018), and promotes the removal of catenations between chromosomes and sister-chromatids by orientating the activity of topoisomerase II (Topo II) toward decatenation (Baxter et al., 2011; Charbin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on condensin function and includes some inference about the mechanisms.

claim: When condensin is impaired, sister-centromeres often reach the opposite poles of the mitotic spindle in anaphase but chromosome arms fail to separate, forming stereotypical chromatin bridges.
source: Hence, when condensin is impaired, sister-centromeres often reach the opposite poles of the mitotic spindle in anaphase but chromosome arms fail to separate, forming stereotypical chromatin bridges.
evidence: The claim is based on established observations of condensin mutant phenotypes.

claim: Condensin anchors itself on naked DNA through sequence-independent electrostatic interactions and uses the energy of ATP hydrolysis to extrude adjacent DNA segments into a loop of increasing size.
source: In vitro studies have shown that condensin anchors itself on naked DNA through sequence-independent electrostatic interactions and uses the energy of ATP hydrolysis to extrude adjacent DNA segments into a loop of increasing size (Kschonsak et al., 2017; Ganji et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies demonstrating condensin's loop extrusion activity.

claim: ChIP-seq studies have revealed a conserved condensin pattern along the genome, constituted of a broad and basal distribution punctuated by peaks of high occupancy at centromeres, rDNA repeats, and in the vicinity of highly expressed genes.
source: ChIP-sequencing (ChIP-seq) studies performed on species ranging from yeasts to mammals have revealed a conserved condensin pattern along the genome, constituted of a broad and basal distribution punctuated by peaks of high occupancy at centromeres, rDNA repeats, and in the vicinity of highly expressed genes (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2013; Kranz et al., 2013; Dowen et al., 2013; Sutani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple ChIP-seq studies across different species.

claim: Various factors such as the chromokinesin Kif4, the zinc-finger protein AKAP95, transcription factors, and chromatin remodelers have been involved in the binding of condensin to chromatin in yeasts or vertebrate cells.
source: Various factors such as the chromokinesin Kif4 (Samejima et al., 2012), the zinc-finger protein AKAP95 (Steen et al., 2000), transcription factors, and chromatin remodelers (for review see Robellet et al., 2017) have been involved in the binding of condensin to chromatin in yeasts or vertebrate cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies identifying factors involved in condensin binding.

claim: Condensin contributes to the stiffness of centromeric chromatin and to the bilateral attachment of centromeres in early mitosis.
source: Such enrichments are likely to play a positive role since there is clear evidence that condensin contributes to the stiffness of centromeric chromatin and to the bilateral attachment of centromeres in early mitosis (Ono et al., 2004; Gerlich et al., 2006; Nakazawa et al., 2008; Ribeiro et al., 2009; Verzijlbergen et al., 2014; Piskadlo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating condensin's role at centromeres.

claim: The segregation of the rDNA is acutely sensitive to condensin activity.
source: Likewise, the segregation of the rDNA is acutely sensitive to condensin activity (Freeman et al., 2000; Nakazawa et al., 2008; Samoshkin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing rDNA segregation defects in condensin mutants.

claim: Highly expressed genes are thought to constitute a permeable barrier where active condensin complexes stall upon encounters with DNA-bound factors such as RNA polymerases.
source: Highly expressed genes, in contrast, are thought to constitute a permeable barrier where active condensin complexes stall upon encounters with DNA-bound factors such as RNA polymerases (Brandão et al., 2019; Rivosecchi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies proposing this mechanism.

claim: Attenuating transcription that persists during mitosis improves chromosome segregation when condensin is impaired in fission yeast.
source: Consistent with a local hindrance, in fission yeast, attenuating transcription that persists during mitosis improves chromosome segregation when condensin is impaired (Sutani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study in fission yeast.

claim: Dense arrays of protein tightly bound to DNA can constitute a barrier for DNA-translocating condensin in budding yeast.
source: Further evidence in budding yeast indicates that dense arrays of protein tightly bound to DNA can constitute a barrier for DNA-translocating condensin (Guérin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study in budding yeast.

claim: Condensin I is enriched at telomeres during mitosis and meiosis in mammalian cells.
source: Microscopy studies have clearly shown that condensin I is enriched at telomeres during mitosis and meiosis in mammalian cells (Walther et al., 2018; Viera et al., 2007), and ChIP-seq has further revealed that condensin I accumulates at telomere repeats in chicken DT40 cells, but the mechanisms underlying such enrichment as well as its functional significance have remained unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to microscopy and ChIP-seq studies in mammalian cells.

claim: The separation of sister-telomeres in anaphase involves condensin regulators such as Cdc14 phosphatase in budding yeast and Aurora-B kinase in fission yeast.
source: We and others previously showed that the separation of sister-telomeres in anaphase involves condensin regulators such as Cdc14 phosphatase in budding yeast (Clemente-Blanco et al., 2011), and Aurora-B kinase in fission yeast (Reyes et al., 2015; Berthezene et al., 2020), but whether and how condensin could play a role has remained unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors and others.

claim: Telomeres contain G-rich repetitive sequences that are protected by a conserved protein complex called Shelterin.
source: Telomeres contain G-rich repetitive sequences that are protected by a conserved protein complex called Shelterin (de Lange, 2018; Lim and Cech, 2021), which is composed, in fission yeast, of Taz1 (a myb-domain DNA-binding protein homologous to human TRF1 and TRF2), Rap1, Poz1 (a possible analog of TIN2), Tpz1 (an ortholog of TPP1), Pot1, and Ccq1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reviews on shelterin and established knowledge about telomere structure.

claim: Taz1 binds to double-stranded G-rich telomeric repeats.
source: While Taz1 binds to double-stranded G-rich telomeric repeats, Pot1 binds to 3′ single-stranded overhang.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Taz1 function.

claim: Pot1 binds to 3′ single-stranded overhang.
source: While Taz1 binds to double-stranded G-rich telomeric repeats, Pot1 binds to 3′ single-stranded overhang.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Pot1 function.

claim: Rap1, Poz1, and Tpz1 act as a molecular bridge connecting Taz1 and Pot1 through protein-protein interactions.
source: Rap1, Poz1, and Tpz1 act as a molecular bridge connecting Taz1 and Pot1 through protein-protein interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about shelterin complex organization.

claim: Ccq1 contributes to the recruitment of the nucleosome remodeler Mit1 and of telomerase.
source: Ccq1 contributes to the recruitment of the nucleosome remodeler Mit1 and of telomerase (for review on fission yeast shelterin see Moser and Nakamura, 2009; Dehé and Cooper, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reviews on fission yeast shelterin.

claim: Taz1 plays the role of a cis-acting enrichment factor for condensin at telomeres.
source: We found that Taz1 plays the role of a cis-acting enrichment factor for condensin at telomeres, while Mit1 antagonizes condensin's accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing reduced condensin binding at telomeres in taz1Δ cells.

claim: Mit1 antagonizes condensin's accumulation at telomeres.
source: We found that Taz1 plays the role of a cis-acting enrichment factor for condensin at telomeres, while Mit1 antagonizes condensin's accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing increased condensin binding at telomeres in mit1Δ cells.

claim: The level of condensin at telomeres, set up by Taz1 and Mit1, is instrumental for their proper disjunction during anaphase.
source: Our results further indicate that the level of condensin at telomeres, set up by Taz1 and Mit1, is instrumental for their proper disjunction during anaphase, hence associating a key biological function to this local enrichment.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that modulating condensin levels at telomeres affects telomere separation efficiency.

claim: Fission yeast condensin is largely cytoplasmic during interphase and binds genomic DNA during mitosis.
source: Fission yeast condensin, like vertebrate condensin I, is largely cytoplasmic during interphase and binds genomic DNA during mitosis (Sutani et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on fission yeast condensin localization.

claim: Fission yeast condensin shows high level of occupancy at centromeres, at rDNA repeats and in the vicinity of highly transcribed genes during mitosis.
source: At this stage, it shows high level of occupancy at centromeres, at rDNA repeats and in the vicinity of highly transcribed genes (Sutani et al., 2015; Nakazawa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to ChIP-seq studies in fission yeast.

claim: Cnd2-GFP was hardly detectable at TEL2R and along chromosome arms during the G2 arrest.
source: Cnd2-GFP was hardly detectable at TEL2R and along chromosome arms during the G2 arrest (Figure 1B, t=0 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During early mitosis, Cnd2-GFP was clearly bound to telomeric repeats (the tel0 site), and to a lesser extent at more distal sites within sub-telomeric elements.
source: However, during early mitosis, Cnd2-GFP was clearly bound to telomeric repeats (the tel0 site), and to a lesser extent at more distal sites within sub-telomeric elements (Figure 1B, t=7 min post-release).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cnd2-GFP occupancy at tel0 was in the range of the highly expressed genes cdc22 and exg1.
source: Cnd2-GFP occupancy at tel0 was in the range of the highly expressed genes cdc22 and exg1 used as control for enrichment (Sutani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cnd2-GFP level further increased in anaphase (15 min post-release from the G2 block).
source: Cnd2-GFP level further increased in anaphase (15 min post-release from the G2 block), consistent with the maximum folding of fission yeast chromosomes achieved in anaphase (Petrova et al., 2013) and reminiscent of the second wave of condensin binding observed during anaphase in human cells (Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and citations to related studies.

claim: The cut14-208 mutation reduced the binding of Cnd2-GFP at centromeres, along chromosome arms, and at TEL2R.
source: Consistent with previous ChIP-qPCR data (Nakazawa et al., 2015), we found that the cut14-208 mutation reduced the binding of Cnd2-GFP at centromeres (Figure 1C), along chromosome arms (Figure 1D), and at TEL2R (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cut3-477 mutation caused genome-wide reduction in Cnd2-GFP binding, though of a smaller amplitude at TEL2R.
source: We observed similar genome-wide reduction in cut3-477 cells, though of a smaller amplitude at TEL2R (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: cut14-208 cells shifted to 36°C almost never showed more than six telomeric dots in anaphase, despite their centromeres being segregated at the opposite poles of the mitotic spindle.
source: Strikingly, cut14-208 cells shifted to 36°C almost never showed more than six telomeric dots in anaphase, despite their centromeres being segregated at the opposite poles of the mitotic spindle (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Sister-telomere disjunction was also clearly impaired in cut3-477 mutant cells, though at milder level.
source: Sister-telomere disjunction was also clearly impaired in cut3-477 mutant cells, though at milder level (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After anaphase onset, control cells always displayed two sister telomeric 1L foci (n=43) while 82% of cut14-208 mutant cells (n=51) grown at non-permissive temperature remained with a single telomeric foci.
source: After anaphase onset, as judged by the separation of sister-centromeres 3L, control cells always displayed two sister telomeric 1L foci (n=43) while 82% of cut14-208 mutant cells (n=51) grown at non-permissive temperature remained with a single telomeric foci confirming a striking defect in the disjunction of Tel1L.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Telomere disjunction remained effective during anaphase at 19°C in top2-250 mutant cells, even within chromatin bridges.
source: Yet, and remarkably, telomere disjunction remained effective during anaphase at 19°C, even within chromatin bridges (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The decatenation activity of Topo II and the full separation of chromosome arms are largely dispensable for telomere disjunction.
source: The decatenation activity of Topo II and the full separation of chromosome arms are therefore largely dispensable for telomere disjunction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that telomeres separate in top2-250 mutant cells despite chromatin bridges.

claim: Contact frequencies between telomeres were increased in the cut14-208 condensin mutant at restrictive temperature, both within chromosomes (intra) and in-between chromosomes (inter).
source: In contrast, contacts frequencies between telomeres were increased, both within chromosomes (intra) and in-between chromosomes (inter) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Intra-chromosomal contacts dominate over inter-chromosomal contacts at telomeres in wild-type cells and were increased in the cut14-208 mutant.
source: Aggregating Hi-C signals at chromosome ends further revealed that intra-chromosomal contacts dominate over inter-chromosomal contacts in wild-type cells and were increased in the mutant (Figure 3E, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by aggregated Hi-C data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Fission yeast chromosomes enter mitosis in a Rabl configuration, with telomeres clustered together.
source: Taken together these data suggest that fission yeast chromosomes enter mitosis in a Rabl configuration, with telomeres clustered together and that condensin drives their declustering into pairs of sister-telomeres as cells progress toward metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and their full separation in anaphase (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Hi-C data showing increased telomere-telomere contacts in condensin mutants.

claim: Condensin drives the declustering of telomeres into pairs of sister-telomeres as cells progress toward metaphase.
source: Taken together these data suggest that fission yeast chromosomes enter mitosis in a Rabl configuration, with telomeres clustered together and that condensin drives their declustering into pairs of sister-telomeres as cells progress toward metaphase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and their full separation in anaphase (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Hi-C data showing increased telomere clustering in condensin mutants.

claim: In cells lacking Taz1, Cnd2-GFP occupancy was reduced almost twofold at telomeres (tel0 site) and sub-telomeres (tel2.4 site), while remaining unchanged at the kinetochore and within chromosome arms.
source: In cells lacking Taz1, Cnd2-GFP occupancy was reduced almost twofold at telomeres (tel0 site) and sub-telomeres (tel2.4 site), while remaining unchanged at the kinetochore and within chromosome arms.
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rap1Δ mutant showed no change in Cnd2-GFP occupancy compared to wild-type.
source: In contrast, the rap1∆ mutant showed no change compared to wild-type.
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The binding of Cnd2-GFP was basal and independent of Taz1 at non-telomeric Taz1-islands.
source: However, the binding of Cnd2-GFP was basal and independent of Taz1 at such non-telomeric Taz1-islands (Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C), suggesting that Taz1 is unlikely to directly recruit condensin onto chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B, C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: No physical interaction was observed between condensin and Taz1, either by co-IP or by yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: In line with this, we observed no physical interaction between condensin and Taz1, either by co-IP or by yeast two-hybrid assay (our unpublished data).
evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished experimental data from the authors.

claim: Mit1 maintains nucleosome occupancy through its association with the shelterin.
source: Indeed, Mit1 maintains nucleosome occupancy through its association with the shelterin and mit1∆ cells show a reduced histone H3 occupancy at sub-telomeres (van Emden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on Mit1 function.

claim: mit1Δ cells show a reduced histone H3 occupancy at sub-telomeres.
source: Indeed, Mit1 maintains nucleosome occupancy through its association with the shelterin and mit1∆ cells show a reduced histone H3 occupancy at sub-telomeres (van Emden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on Mit1 function.

claim: An increased condensin occupancy at telomeres and sub-telomeres was observed in cells lacking Mit1.
source: As expected, we observed an increased condensin occupancy at telomeres and sub-telomeres by calibrated ChIP-seq (Figure 4D) and ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increase in condensin occupancy in mit1Δ cells was largely, if not strictly, restricted to chromosome ends.
source: ChIP-seq further showed that such increase was largely, if not strictly, restricted to chromosome ends (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4D, E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Very few non-disjunction events were observed during anaphases in taz1Δ single mutant cells at 32°C.
source: We observed very few non-disjunction events during anaphases in taz1∆ single mutant cells at 32°C (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Combining cut3-477 and taz1Δ caused a synergistic increase of the frequency of sister-telomere non-disjunction.
source: However, combining cut3-477 and taz1∆ caused a synergistic increase of the frequency of sister-telomere non-disjunction (Figure 5A) that correlated with a synthetic negative growth defect at 32°C and 34°C (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and growth assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Eliminating Mit1 rescued sister-telomere disjunction in cut3-477 mutant cells.
source: Conversely, eliminating Mit1 rescued sister-telomere disjunction in cut3-477 mutant cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Eliminating the heterochromatin protein Swi6HP1 alleviates the telomere separation defect caused by the inhibition of Ark1.
source: We previously showed that eliminating the heterochromatin protein Swi6HP1 alleviates the telomere separation defect caused by the inhibition of Ark1 (Reyes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Ark1 controls condensin association with chromosomes.
source: Since Ark1 controls condensin association with chromosomes (Petersen and Hagan, 2003; Tada et al., 2011), and Swi6 enriches cohesin at heterochromatin domains, including telomeres (Bernard et al., 2001), we asked whether interplays between condensin and cohesin might underlie telomere separation during anaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on Ark1 function.

claim: Swi6 enriches cohesin at heterochromatin domains, including telomeres.
source: Since Ark1 controls condensin association with chromosomes (Petersen and Hagan, 2003; Tada et al., 2011), and Swi6 enriches cohesin at heterochromatin domains, including telomeres (Bernard et al., 2001), we asked whether interplays between condensin and cohesin might underlie telomere separation during anaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on Swi6 function.

claim: Sister-telomere separation occurs at a smaller mitotic spindle size in the rad21-K1 mutant as compared to wild-type.
source: First, we observed that sister-telomere separation occurs at a smaller mitotic spindle size in the rad21-K1 mutant as compared to wild-type, indicating an accelerated kinetics during mitosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Weakening cohesin partly rescued telomere disjunction when condensin was impaired, as suggested by the increased number of telomeric dots displayed by cut3-477 rad21-K1 double mutant cells in anaphase.
source: Second, weakening cohesin partly rescued telomere disjunction when condensin was impaired, as suggested by the increased number of telomeric dots displayed by cut3-477 rad21-K1 double mutant cells in anaphase (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A strong increase in Psm3-GFP levels at telomeres (tel0 site) and sub-telomeres (tel1.2 site) was observed in cut3-477 mutant cells, but no change at further distal sites, nor within chromosome arms or at centromeres.
source: In cut3-477 mutant cells, however, we observed a strong increase in Psm3-GFP levels at telomeres (tel0 site) and sub-telomeres (tel1.2 site), but no change at further distal sites, nor within chromosome arms or at centromeres (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The specific increase in cohesin occupancy at telomeres and sub-telomeres in the condensin mutant was readily visible both during G2 and anaphase.
source: This specific increase in occupancy at telomeres and sub-telomeres in the condensin mutant was readily visible both during G2 and anaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by calibrated ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cohesin restrains telomere disjunction in anaphase.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that cohesin restrains telomere disjunction in anaphase and that condensin prevents the accumulation of cohesin at telomeres.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic and ChIP data showing that weakening cohesin rescues telomere separation defects in condensin mutants.

claim: Condensin prevents the accumulation of cohesin at telomeres.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that cohesin restrains telomere disjunction in anaphase and that condensin prevents the accumulation of cohesin at telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing increased cohesin at telomeres in condensin mutants.

claim: The kleisin subunit of condensin II (CAPH2) binds human TRF1 in RPE-1 cells.
source: Previous work has shown that the kleisin subunit of condensin II (CAPH2) binds human TRF1, a counterpart of Taz1, in RPE-1 cells (Wallace et al., 2019), but since no physical or functional link has been described between TRF1 and other subunits of the condensin II holocomplex, it was unclear whether CAPH2 might act at telomeres independently of condensin II.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on CAPH2 and TRF1 interaction.

claim: The kleisin subunit of fission yeast condensin is bound to the telomere repeats of TEL2R in metaphase and anaphase.
source: Here, we show that the kleisin subunit of fission yeast condensin is bound to the telomere repeats of TEL2R in metaphase and anaphase and that such binding relies on the Cut14SMC2 and Cut3SMC4 ATPases (Saka et al., 1994), arguing therefore that the condensin holocomplex is bound to TEL2R.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing Cnd2-GFP binding at TEL2R and its dependence on Cut14 and Cut3.

claim: Chromosome I and II contains similar sub-telomeric elements.
source: Since southern blotting and FISH experiments have shown that chromosome I and II contains similar sub-telomeric elements (Funabiki et al., 1993; Oizumi et al., 2021), our observations made using TEL2R DNA are likely to be relevant to most fission yeast telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on fission yeast telomere structure.

claim: Deleting Rap1 does not impair condensin localization at telomeres.
source: First, the fact that deleting Rap1, another key component of shelterin, does not impair condensin localization and, second, our finding that condensin binding to telomeres is also controlled, negatively, by the nucleosome remodeler Mit1, which associates with telomeres via the Ccq1 subunit of shelterin (Sugiyama et al., 2007; van Emden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing no change in condensin binding in rap1Δ cells.

claim: Mit1 associates with telomeres via the Ccq1 subunit of shelterin.
source: First, the fact that deleting Rap1, another key component of shelterin, does not impair condensin localization and, second, our finding that condensin binding to telomeres is also controlled, negatively, by the nucleosome remodeler Mit1, which associates with telomeres via the Ccq1 subunit of shelterin (Sugiyama et al., 2007; van Emden et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on Mit1 localization.

claim: No protein-to-protein interactions were detected between Taz1 and Cnd2/condensin.
source: However, and in sharp contrast with the human TRF1 and CAP-H2 (Wallace et al., 2019), we detected no protein-to-protein interactions between Taz1 and Cnd2/condensin.
evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished experimental data from the authors.

claim: Taz1 does not enrich condensin at discrete Taz1-DNA binding sites located outside telomeres.
source: Together with our observation that Taz1 does not enrich condensin at discrete Taz1-DNA binding sites located outside telomeres, this suggests that Taz1 is not a cis-acting recruiter for condensin at telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data showing no condensin enrichment at non-telomeric Taz1 islands.

claim: Arrays of Taz1 proteins tightly bound to telomere repeats might create a permeable barrier onto which condensin molecules accumulate.
source: Rather, by analogy with the accumulation of condensin at highly expressed genes (Brandão et al., 2019; Rivosecchi et al., 2021), we speculate that arrays of Taz1 proteins tightly bound to telomere repeats might create a permeable barrier onto which condensin molecules accumulate.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on analogy with condensin behavior at highly expressed genes.

claim: Condensin promotes the dissociation of telomeric clusters inherited from the Rabl organization of chromosomes in interphase by folding chromatin into mitotic chromosomes.
source: It is tempting to speculate that condensin promotes the dissociation of telomeric clusters, inherited from the Rabl organization of chromosomes in interphase, by folding chromatin into mitotic chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from Hi-C data showing increased telomere clustering in condensin mutants.

claim: The existence of a dedicated pathway for sister-telomere disjunction is a conserved feature of eukaryotic cells.
source: This finding is reminiscent of telomere separation in human cells that specifically relies on the activity of the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase tankyrase 1 (Dynek and Smith, 2004), and suggest therefore that the existence of a dedicated pathway for sister-telomere disjunction is a conserved feature of eukaryotic cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison with human cells and supported by a citation.

claim: Failures to disjoin sister-telomeres most likely contribute to the stereotypical chromatin bridge phenotype exhibited by condensin-defective cells.
source: The corollary is that failures to disjoin sister-telomeres most likely contribute to the stereotypical chromatin bridge phenotype exhibited by condensin-defective cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that condensin mutants show both telomere separation defects and chromatin bridges.

claim: Topo II catalytic activity is dispensable for telomere segregation provided that condensin is active.
source: Our results do not rule out the possibility that Topo II contributes to telomeres disentanglements, but nevertheless imply that Topo II catalytic activity is dispensable for telomere segregation provided that condensin is active.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that telomeres separate in top2-250 mutant cells.

claim: The close proximity of DNA ends could explain the dispensability of Topo II for telomere segregation.
source: The close proximity of DNA ends could explain such a dispensability.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible explanation for the observation.

claim: The segregation of LacO repeats inserted in the vicinity of TelV is impaired by the top2-4 mutation in budding yeast.
source: It has been reported in budding yeast that the segregation of LacO repeats inserted in the vicinity of TelV is impaired by the top2-4 mutation (Bhalla et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study in budding yeast.

claim: LacO arrays tightly bound by LacI proteins constitute a barrier for the recoiling activity of budding yeast condensin in anaphase.
source: However, since LacO arrays tightly bound by LacI proteins constitute a barrier for the recoiling activity of budding yeast condensin in anaphase (Guérin et al., 2019), the insertion of such a construct might have created an experimental condition in which condensin activity was specifically impaired at TELV, hence revealing the contribution of Topo II.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on condensin and LacO arrays.

claim: The telomere structure in budding and fission yeast is significantly different.
source: In addition, the telomere structure in budding and fission yeast is significantly different.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about telomere structure differences between yeast species.

claim: Budding yeast protects its telomeres via two independent factors, Rap1 and the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 complex.
source: Budding yeast protects its telomeres via two independent factors, Rap1 and the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 complex, whereas in fission yeast Taz1 and Pot1 are bridged by a complex protein interaction network (Rap1-Poz1-Tpz1).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about budding yeast telomere protection.

claim: In fission yeast Taz1 and Pot1 are bridged by a complex protein interaction network (Rap1-Poz1-Tpz1).
source: Budding yeast protects its telomeres via two independent factors, Rap1 and the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 complex, whereas in fission yeast Taz1 and Pot1 are bridged by a complex protein interaction network (Rap1-Poz1-Tpz1).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about fission yeast shelterin structure.

claim: The telomeric components of S. pombe can dimerize leading to a higher complex organization of the shelterin.
source: Notably, it was recently shown that the telomeric components of S. pombe can dimerize leading to a higher complex organization of the shelterin (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recent study on shelterin organization.

claim: Dimerization of Taz1, Poz1, and the Tpz1-Ccq1 subcomplex may contribute to the clustering of sister and non-sister-chromatid telomeres.
source: It is thus likely that dimerization of Taz1, Poz1, and the Tpz1-Ccq1 subcomplex may also contribute to the clustering of sister and non-sister-chromatid telomeres.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of shelterin dimerization.

claim: Cohesin has been involved in telomere cohesion in budding yeast.
source: Cohesin has been involved in telomere cohesion in budding yeast (Antoniacci and Skibbens, 2006; Renshaw et al., 2010), but in human cells the situation remains unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies in budding yeast.

claim: Scc3SA1 is a likely target of the tankyrase 1 pathway for telomere disjunction in human cells.
source: Although Scc3SA1 is a likely target of the tankyrase 1 pathway for telomere disjunction (Canudas and Smith, 2009), telomeric cohesion appears independent of other cohesin subunits (Bisht et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on tankyrase 1 and cohesin in human cells.

claim: Telomeric cohesion appears independent of other cohesin subunits in human cells.
source: Although Scc3SA1 is a likely target of the tankyrase 1 pathway for telomere disjunction (Canudas and Smith, 2009), telomeric cohesion appears independent of other cohesin subunits (Bisht et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on telomeric cohesion in human cells.

claim: rad21-K1 accelerates sister-telomere disjunction in an otherwise wild-type genetic background.
source: Our finding that rad21-K1, a loss-of-function mutation in the kleisin subunit of fission yeast cohesin, accelerates sister-telomere disjunction in an otherwise wild-type genetic background would be consistent with a role for cohesin in ensuring cohesion between sister-telomeres in fission yeast.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing accelerated telomere separation in rad21-K1 mutant cells.

claim: The kinetics of sister-telomere disjunction is not accelerated in cells lacking the core heterochromatin protein Swi6.
source: However, such an indirect effect seems less likely because the kinetics of sister-telomere disjunction is not accelerated in cells lacking the core heterochromatin protein Swi6 (Reyes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The shelterin complex may link sister-telomeres together.
source: Because of its ability to organize telomeres into various structures (Lim and Cech, 2021), the shelterin complex may link sister-telomeres together and loop extrusion by condensin may provide the power stroke to disentangle such structures.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on known properties of shelterin.

claim: Loop extrusion by condensin may provide the power stroke to disentangle structures linking sister-telomeres.
source: Because of its ability to organize telomeres into various structures (Lim and Cech, 2021), the shelterin complex may link sister-telomeres together and loop extrusion by condensin may provide the power stroke to disentangle such structures.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for condensin action at telomeres.

claim: The accumulation of condensin against Taz1TRF1-2 barriers, together with a possible up-regulation by Aurora-B kinase in anaphase, might allow condensin-mediated DNA translocation to pass a threshold beyond which the ties between sister-telomeres would be eliminated.
source: Thus, as speculated in Figure 7, the accumulation of condensin against Taz1TRF1-2 barriers, together with a possible up-regulation by Aurora-B kinase in anaphase (Reyes et al., 2015), might allow condensin-mediated DNA translocation to pass a threshold beyond which the ties between sister-telomeres would be eliminated, be it cohesin- and/or shelterin-mediated.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a model for how condensin drives telomere separation.

claim: Given the conservation of shelterin, and the abundance of condensin complexes at telomeres during mitosis and meiosis in mammals, condensin specifically drives the separation of telomeres in other living organisms.
source: Whatever the mechanism, given the conservation of shelterin, and the abundance of condensin complexes at telomeres during mitosis and meiosis in mammals (Viera et al., 2007; Walther et al., 2018), we speculate that condensin specifically drives the separation of telomeres in other living organisms.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from fission yeast findings to other organisms.
